input.step_by_step_reasoning: 1) Nodes: all 10 world-model entities are kept. The drone is kept as the system entry point and as an endpoint of a ledger edge. The three Lambda functions perform distinct Step Functions stages (check for new imagery, pull to S3, create raster proxies), so they stay separate. The third-party imagery software and the on-premises server and database are mapped to ThirdParty. No extra nodes were invented. 2) Flows: Flow 0 = drone imagery capture and third-party processing. Flow 1 = scheduled ingestion pipeline (CloudWatch event -> Step Functions -> three Lambdas -> S3 -> raster proxies in the on-prem database). Flow 2 = end-user viewing through the on-prem mapping software, via Storage Gateway, to S3. 3) Edge types: control for the schedule trigger and Step Functions invocations; meta for API polling, return/completion and acknowledgement arrows; data for payload transfers. Directions follow the ledger; reverse arrows the audio does not describe are still emitted. 4) Ledger self-check: visual_connections has 20 entries; 20 edges are emitted, one per entry with the same source and target. No extra edges were added.

graph.name: Marathon Oil: Serverless Drone Imagery Processing for Well Pad Monitoring
graph.categories: Serverless, Storage, Hybrid, Energy, Image Processing
graph.notes: Drones flown by licensed third-party pilots capture well pad imagery, which third-party software processes into three files per well pad. A scheduled CloudWatch event starts a Step Functions workflow of three Lambda functions: check for new imagery via API, pull images into S3, and create raster proxies stored in the on-premises database. The on-prem mapping software reads the images from S3 via Storage Gateway for maintenance and operations teams.

nodes.name: Drone
nodes.notes: Drones flown by licensed third-party pilots routinely capture imagery of every well pad (replacing manual inspections by people).

nodes.name: Third-party imagery processing software
nodes.notes: Processes drone imagery into three files per well pad: an orthomosaic (high-resolution top-down view), a digital terrain model and a digital elevation model. Files are stored on the third-party server and exposed via an API.

nodes.name: CloudWatch Event
nodes.notes: Scheduled event that starts the Step Functions workflow.

nodes.name: Step Functions
nodes.notes: Workflow of three Lambda functions: check whether new imagery is available, pull images from the third party to S3, create raster proxies.

nodes.name: Lambda - check for new imagery
nodes.notes: First Lambda: calls the third-party software API to determine whether new images or flights are available.

nodes.name: Lambda - pull imagery to S3
nodes.notes: Second Lambda: invoked when a new flight or image is found; takes the images from the third party and stores them in an S3 bucket in Marathon Oil's environment.

nodes.name: Lambda - create raster proxies
nodes.notes: Third Lambda: takes the S3 images and creates raster proxies, which act like URLs telling the on-prem server how to fetch the images. No application change is needed on-premises.

nodes.name: S3
nodes.notes: Bucket holding the processed imagery data pulled from the third party.

nodes.name: Storage Gateway
nodes.notes: Lets the on-premises mapping software read image files from the S3 bucket.

nodes.name: On-premises database & server (mapping software)
nodes.notes: The database stores the raster proxies; the server handles user queries. The mapping software cannot read imagery directly from S3 without raster proxies. Used by maintenance and operations teams to spot equipment issues, plan preventative maintenance and check well pad health.
